title: What Is India's First Tokenized Bond and Can You Buy It?

content:
India's first tokenized corporate bond went live for a pilot in September 2026, issued by state-owned REC Limited and settled in the RBI's wholesale digital rupee. It's a genuinely significant moment for how Indian debt markets work. But if you're checking whether you can buy some on Zerodha right now: you can't. The pilot is closed to retail investors and limited to a small group of institutional participants. Here's what's actually happening, and what it might mean for your portfolio later.

Key Takeaways

  • REC Limited is issuing up to ₹500 crore in tokenized bonds, settled via the RBI's wholesale digital rupee
  • Retail investors are locked out of the September pilot; only select institutional investors can participate
  • Settlement drops from T+2 business days to near-instant, the main practical improvement
  • Investors need two new accounts: a wholesale CBDC wallet and a DEMAT 2.0 wallet
  • Secondary market trading is expected by December 2026; broad retail access may follow in 2027

What Is a Tokenized Bond, Exactly?

A tokenized bond records ownership and settlement on a blockchain rather than in a traditional registrar's ledger. When you buy one, your ownership is a digital token. Settlement, which normally takes two business days in India, becomes near-instant. The underlying asset is still a bond, so the issuer's credit risk is unchanged.

Think of it as the bond equivalent of moving from paper share certificates to electronic DEMAT records in the late 1990s. That shift didn't change what a share was worth; it changed how quickly and cheaply you could trade it. Tokenization does the same for bonds, but goes one step further by using a blockchain to cut out the central clearinghouse.

Regular bonds in India settle on a T+2 cycle. Buy on Monday, and the exchange of money and security happens on Wednesday. Tokenized bonds compress that to seconds. Abstract until you're a fund manager moving hundreds of crores daily and one extra day of float costs you.

Can Regular Investors Buy India's First Tokenized Bond?

Not right now. The September 2026 pilot is restricted to a select group of institutional investors, and retail participation hasn't been announced. You'd also need a wholesale CBDC wallet, which banks haven't opened for retail customers. Secondary market trading, which could eventually let retail investors in, is planned for December 2026.

This is the bit most news coverage glosses over. Headlines say India launched tokenized bonds without noting that a regular investor with a Zerodha or Groww account is completley locked out of the pilot.

The barriers are structural. The settlement currency for this pilot is the RBI's wholesale digital rupee, distinct from the retail e-rupee. Wholesale CBDC wallets are opened by banks for institutional counterparties only. On top of that, CDSL and NSDL are building a new DEMAT 2.0 system for tokenized securities that doesn't connect to your existing DEMAT account.

So two separate infrastructure layers need to be built and made retail-accessible before you can participate. That takes time.

What Does This Mean for Bonds You Already Hold?

Nothing changes for now. Bonds you already hold in your DEMAT account continue to operate under the existing system. The tokenized bond pilot is additive, not a replacement. If the technology eventually scales to mainstream markets, the transition would be gradual and handled by depositories in the background.

If you hold REC bonds, Bharat Bond ETFs, or any corporate bonds through a regular brokerage, those are entirely unaffected. They'll settle and mature exactly as before.

The pilot is a seperate experiment running alongside the existing infrastructure, not a migration. The scenario where this becomes relevant for you is if and when SEBI and the RBI allow tokenized bonds into the mainstream market. Based on how similar pilots have played out elsewhere, that could take two to three years. The European Investment Bank first issued a blockchain bond in 2021; broad retail access to tokenized debt instruments remains limited even now across most markets.

Is This a Good Investment, If You Could Buy It?

As a bond, REC's offering is probably fine. REC Limited is AAA-rated by domestic credit agencies and has the government of India as a major shareholder. That credit profile doesn't change because the bond is tokenized. The real unknowns are the new settlement infrastructure and the still-developing secondary market.

The technology risk is the more interesting question. Blockchain settlement systems can fail due to network congestion or smart contract bugs. In a small pilot with institutional participants, any glitch gets caught and fixed quietly. At retail scale, the exposure would be far larger.

That said, getting worried about blockchain risk on a government-backed issuer's limited pilot is probaly premature. The whole point of a limited pilot is to surface problems before they matter at scale. RBI and SEBI have been cautious about this, which is reassuring.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the REC tokenized bond?

REC Limited, a government-owned power finance company, is issuing up to ₹500 crore in digital bonds in September 2026. Ownership records and settlement run on a blockchain, with payments made in the RBI's wholesale digital rupee. It's India's first corporate bond issued and settled this way.

What is DEMAT 2.0?

DEMAT 2.0 is a new digital wallet system that India's depositories, CDSL and NSDL, are building to hold tokenized securities on distributed ledger technology. It's separate from your existing DEMAT account. You'll need one to invest in tokenized bonds once retail access opens, though no date has been confirmed.

When can retail investors buy tokenized bonds in India?

There's no confirmed date yet. Secondary market trading for the REC pilot is expected by December 2026, but whether retail brokerages will be able to access that market hasn't been announced. Broad retail access may take until 2027 or later, based on how the pilot develops.

Are tokenized bonds safer than regular bonds?

Credit safety depends on the issuer, not the format. A tokenized REC bond carries the same credit risk as a regular REC bond. Tokenization adds technology-related risks (smart contract bugs, network congestion) while potentially reducing settlement and counterparty risks. The net effect is roughly neutral for a well-run pilot.

What is India's wholesale digital rupee?

The wholesale CBDC is a digital form of the rupee issued by the RBI for interbank and institutional transactions. It's different from the retail e-rupee designed for consumer payments. The REC bond pilot uses wholesale CBDC for settlement between institutional participants, not a system regular bank accounts connect to.

What does T+2 settlement mean in bonds?

T+2 means the actual transfer of money and securities happens two business days after a trade. Buy a bond on Monday, and legal ownership and payment settle by Wednesday. Tokenized bonds enable near-instant atomic settlement where asset and payment are exchanged simultaneously, in seconds rather than days.

The Short Version

India's first tokenized corporate bond is a real structural step for how securities settle. Near-instant settlement using the digital rupee is genuinely new. But retail investors can't buy it yet, and nothing about your existing bonds changes. Follow the pilot; don't rush.
